title: Optical Illusions
objective: After this level you can explain why the brain can be fooled by optical illusions.
summary: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality. The Müller-Lyer lines and Adelson's checker-shadow squares show the brain's interpretations misfiring.

cards.headline: Two lines, exactly the same length. One looks longer.
cards.body: Add arrowheads to one line and outward-flaring fins to the other, and the fins win. Your eyes aren't broken. Your brain is interpreting what it sees, and here the interpretation goes wrong.

cards.headline: Seeing isn't measuring
cards.body: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality. Some illusions come from light or poor lighting, some from the eye itself, and many from how your brain processes what the eyes send. The two lines are the Müller-Lyer illusion, published in 1889 by Franz Carl Müller-Lyer: equal lines, but the one with fins flaring outward looks longer. What you see is your brain's reading of the scene, not a ruler's.

cards.headline: The shadow that fools you
cards.body: In Edward Adelson's 1995 checker-shadow illusion, a cylinder casts a shadow across a checkerboard. A square inside the shadow looks much lighter than one outside it, yet they're the exact same grey. Your visual system estimates where the light comes from and judges each surface's own shade, correcting for shadow. On a flat picture that correction misleads you. In the real world, it keeps a white shirt looking white in the shade.

cards.headline: You've been edited all along
cards.body: You've met this editor before. In Level 62 your brain turned the upside-down image on your retina upright, and quietly filled in each eye's blind spot. Illusions aren't a glitch in an otherwise perfect camera. They're the rare moments you catch your brain at work.

cards.headline: Illusions: explained
learned: An illusion is a perception that contradicts reality
Adelson (1995): the brain corrects for shadows
Filling the blind spot is the same editor at work

questions.prompt: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, which of two equal lines looks longer?

options.label: The one drawn in a shadow
options.rationale: Shadows belong to the checker illusion.

options.label: Neither; they look equal
options.rationale: The illusion is that they don't.

options.label: The one with fins flaring outward

questions.explanation: The two lines are the same length, but the one with fins flaring outward looks longer.

questions.prompt: In Adelson's checker-shadow illusion, why does the square in the shadow look lighter than it really is?

options.label: Its paint is lighter than the other square's
options.rationale: They are the exact same grey.

options.label: The brain corrects for a shadow it thinks is there
The blind spot hides part of the picture
Rods take over from cones inside the shadow
options.rationale: It's a flat picture, seen in the same light.

questions.explanation: Your visual system estimates the lighting and judges each surface's own shade, correcting for shadow; on a flat picture the correction misleads.

questions.prompt: From Level 54: if an illusion comes from how your brain processes what the eyes send, which lobes are misreading it?

options.label: The frontal lobes, which plan and drive movement
options.rationale: They plan movement; images go to the back of the brain.

options.label: The temporal lobes, which handle hearing and memory
options.rationale: They handle hearing, not images from the eyes.

options.label: The occipital lobes, which process images from the eyes
The retina, before the signal reaches the brain
options.rationale: The retina isn't a lobe, and these illusions come from the brain's processing.

questions.explanation: Many illusions come from the brain's processing of what the eyes send, and the occipital lobes are where images from the eyes are processed.
